content: The risk of bias was downgraded by two levels due to unclear or high risk of bias across all studies. This included issues with random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, care providers, and outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, baseline group similarity, co-interventions, and compliance with the intervention. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to substantial unexplained heterogeneity, with an I² value of 71%. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to wide confidence intervals that allowed for the possibility of both benefit and no effect, as well as a low number of participants. The risk of bias was again downgraded by two levels in other studies for similar reasons, including unclear or high risk of bias in random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting, and compliance with the intervention. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to considerable unexplained heterogeneity, with an I² value of 87%. For some studies, inconsistency was not assessed because only one study was included in the analysis. Indirectness was downgraded by one level in cases where only one study was included in a subgroup, making it unclear if the findings were representative of all high-income countries. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels in some cases due to wide confidence intervals that allowed for the possibility of harm, no effect, or benefit, as well as a low number of participants. In other instances, imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to the absence of events in either group, or by one level due to small sample sizes that did not meet the optimal information size (OIS). In studies involving transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), the intervention was described as a non-invasive modality using low-voltage electrical currents applied via surface electrodes to modify pain perception. TENS devices were used in both clinical and home settings, with various stimulation parameters tailored to clinical indications. Trials included electrode placement over the paravertebral lumbosacral area and sometimes the affected leg in cases of associated leg pain. Critical outcomes for evaluating interventions included pain, back-specific function/disability, general function/disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, adverse events, medication use, and falls. For older adults, these outcomes were similarly prioritized. No TENS-associated adverse events were reported in any participants across the trials. However, the evidence was often downgraded due to high risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness. For example, inconsistency was downgraded when heterogeneity was substantial (e.g., I² values of 73%, 74%, or higher) and could not be explained by small subgroups. Imprecision was frequently downgraded due to small sample sizes and confidence intervals crossing thresholds for clinical significance. In summary, the evidence for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain, including therapeutic ultrasound and TENS, was limited by methodological concerns, small sample sizes, and heterogeneity across studies. These limitations impacted the reliability of conclusions regarding the benefits and harms of these interventions.
